target: General SWE / backend software engineering internships (big tech + strong startups), 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow tool as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation to make editing smoother, which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred
bullet_feedback.problem: This is the first Capital One bullet a backend reader sees, and it is a desktop UI rebuild: React, TypeScript, Electron, React Flow and Jest are packed into one clause before the reader learns why. The backend-relevant Capital One work (the PostgreSQL/Redis lookup and the sub-skill split) sits below it.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A backend interviewer skimming the second-strongest brand reads this as front-end work first and may pattern-match the internship as UI, even though the stronger backend bullet is two lines down.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: '90% ... preferred' implies preferred over the legacy tool; say so if true
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Reorder Capital One so the PostgreSQL/Redis bullet or the 65% generation-time bullet leads, and move this one to third. Within the bullet, lead with the tool and outcome and drop one of the stacked tech names (Electron or React Flow) to Skills if it does not explain the engineering.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database's permission and rate limits, which became the Claude skill's main search tool
bullet_feedback.problem: 'within the database's permission and rate limits' is ambiguous: 'permission limits' is not a standard concept, so the reader cannot tell whether the cache solved a throttling problem, an access-control problem, or both. It is also the most backend-shaped bullet in the internship but is placed last.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is exactly the bullet a backend interviewer will open with (cache design, invalidation, staleness of precomputed data), and the unclear constraint makes the motivation harder to restate.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 'permission limits' means here (e.g. read-only access, query quotas); how the precomputed tree is refreshed
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name the constraint in plain words before the tech, e.g. 'Because the skill could only query PostgreSQL at a limited rate, precomputed ...'. Move this bullet to the top of Capital One.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-built a topic-scoring research tool and deployed it to dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK to show Amazon Leo's public-policy staff which research topics are popular
bullet_feedback.problem: The middle of the bullet is a tech list ('AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK') with no decision attached, and 'Co-built' plus 'deployed it to dev' leaves the candidate's own share and the tool's status unclear. The purpose arrives only at the end.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A backend interviewer cannot tell whether the candidate wrote the CDK stacks and pipeline or the scoring logic, so the cloud evidence reads as name-dropping rather than ownership.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which part the candidate personally owned (infra as code, pipeline, scoring service)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with what the tool does for the policy staff, then state the candidate's own piece, e.g. 'Wrote the AWS CDK stack and GitHub Actions pipeline that deploy ...'. Keep 'dev' — it is honest scoping.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
bullet_feedback.problem: Strong design-change bullet, but '6,000+ scraped research documents' has no time unit (total corpus vs. per day) and the 34% has no absolute scale (seconds vs. minutes).
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Backend interviewers will immediately ask the throughput and latency numbers; without scale the 34% is harder to anchor on the page.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: is 6,000+ a total or a rate; what the end-to-end latency was before/after if known
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: If known, add the time unit or absolute latency in a few words; otherwise leave as is — the S3-to-Kinesis change is the right thing to emphasize.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of Tortuga's Prisma ORM queries to reduce database load and latency for a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
bullet_feedback.problem: 'to reduce database load and latency' states intent, not result, and the only number (20,000+ visits) measures the product's traffic, not the cache. 'Tortuga' is an unexplained proper noun until 'class scheduler' arrives at the end.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A reader may attribute the 20,000 visits to the caching work, and an interviewer will ask what the cache actually changed; the bullet has no answer on the page.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: any observed change in DB load or response time after the cache, or what was cached and how it was invalidated
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Introduce the product first ('For Tortuga, a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, ...') so the traffic number reads as scale context, then the caching decision (what was cached / invalidation) if no measured result exists.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Building RAG meal suggestions for the official UMD app with SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes, which internal testers rated satisfactory for 93% of meals
bullet_feedback.problem: 'to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes' is a stitched phrase that reads as if GPT-4o mini is being fed meals; the reader has to re-parse to understand that retrieval grounds the model's suggestions in real recipes.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A non-engineer recruiter cannot restate this bullet in one pass, and the key design point (grounding to prevent made-up recipes) is lost.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Rephrase the purpose in plain words, e.g. '... using SentenceBERT search over scraped recipes in ChromaDB so GPT-4o mini suggests real dishes, which ...'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Writing backtested Java capacity-planning logic that sets upper and lower bounds on the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching to balance availability against cost
bullet_feedback.problem: 'the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching' is a reduced relative clause that reads as a noun stack on first pass ('EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves').
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the top bullet on the page under the strongest brand; a one-pass stumble here costs attention in the first seconds of the skim.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Add 'that' to break the noun stack: '... bounds on the EC2 capacity that Amazon Redshift reserves for patching, balancing availability against cost'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp's candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick robot grasps that avoid hitting the table for a PhD-led project targeting ICLR
bullet_feedback.problem: Two trailing purpose clauses ('to help ... that avoid ... for a PhD-led project') make this a long chain; it is also the least backend-relevant item on the page.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Minor for this audience; a backend reader will mostly skip it.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Optional: split the purpose from the project context, or trim 'Built and prompt-tuned' to one verb. Fine to leave as is.

page_feedback.problem: Is the strongest backend/cloud evidence visible first? Partly. AWS SDE Intern at the top is the right headline brand, but its single bullet is in progress with no result, and the next bullet a reader hits is a React/Electron UI rebuild. The clearest backend evidence (PostgreSQL/Redis lookup, S3-to-Kinesis/Lambda latency cut, EventBridge-scheduled eval) and the C++ matching engine sit in the lower two-thirds.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: In a 7-second skim a backend reader sees AWS + Capital One brands but may leave with 'front-end + LLM work' rather than 'systems/backend engineer' — the intended profile.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Reorder Capital One bullets so a backend bullet leads. Section order can stay (experience before projects is correct for these brands).

page_feedback.problem: What a backend interviewer would dig into: cache invalidation and freshness for the Redis category tree and the Tortuga cache; why Kinesis + Lambda over S3 staging (ordering, retries, cost) and what the 34% is measured on; how the LLM-as-judge threshold was chosen; the Redshift backtest methodology; and in the IEX project, single-thread vs. multi-thread at 1.26M events/sec, the 1 mismatched fill of 99,123, and why the B+ tree beat the LSM-tree on reads.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: These are the interview hooks the page creates; every one is a good conversation the candidate should be ready for.

page_feedback.problem: Skills lists REST APIs, API Gateway, Node.js, SQLAlchemy and OpenSearch, none of which appear in any bullet.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: An interviewer who probes a skill not evidenced anywhere may treat the list as padding, which slightly undercuts otherwise strong credibility.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep only skills the candidate can discuss from real work, or ensure the bullets that used them are recognizable (e.g. if the Amazon Leo tool exposes an API, say so).

page_feedback.problem: Heading 'UMD App Development Contracting (Client: Amazon Leo)' puts a second Amazon name directly under the AWS internship.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A fast skimmer may briefly conflate the student contract with Amazon employment; the '(Contract)' title resolves it, so this is minor.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Fine as is; it is already honestly scoped.

keep: Built a C++17 order book and matching engine to replay 50.9M real IEX exchange messages without ever resyncing, which agreed with the exchange on 99,122 of 99,123 fills and 100% of top-of-book prices

Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the engine's event log to compare them on identical 2M-record workloads, which showed the B+ tree giving 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries for 27% more disk
Ran the full replay at 1.26M events/sec end-to-end on an order book that keeps std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map with an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1)
Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting a Claude skill into focused sub-skills that call Python search and validation tools instead of relying on open-ended model search

Built an EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift past a threshold
Co-founded a 110+ member student product studio that has shipped 5 live products
One-page layout, section order (Education, Experience, Projects, Skills) and consistent right-aligned dates/locations
